To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a firm should not be afraid to launch a green product to protect its brown product from the threat of green product cannibalization, as long as the new product is not too green and the brown product is not too brown.

(a) a single pricing scheme can be used to avoid the salience (i.e. the extent) of cannibalization; (b) a single pricing structure can be used to completely avoid cannibalization; but (c) the degree of cannabilzation can be higher for the brown than for the green product when the green segment is sufficiently differentiated.

a firm can never fully avoid cannibalization by revising its pricing structure alone and that the extent of cannibalization between brown and green products can be mitigated by offering differentiated propositions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the strategic implications of the introduction of a new product that is more environmentally friendly.
the pricing, market coverage and production capacity implications of a firm’s product portfolio expansion strategy.
the strategic implications of cannibalization and the tactical ramifications of the pricing strategy for a green product.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a firm should launch a green product only when the value it offers to green segment consumers outweighs the value it takes away from the brown product.
the launch of a new product is always accompanied by cannibalization, but the magnitude of cannibalization can be controlled by the degree of differentiation and the pricing structure.

cannibalization can be mitigated by a two-level pricing structure and that the green product’s presence in a segmented market can only be guaranteed if the firm has sufficient capacity to produce the brown product.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a firm should consider the following factors in order to avoid the negative impact of cannibalization: 1) The firm should be able to differentiate its products in the eyes of green consumers.
a firm can avoid cannibalization and protect its products from each other by revising its pricing structure when resources are abundant, and by expanding its product line when resources are scarce.
cannibalization is not always a bad thing and that a two-level pricing structure is the only means to protect a firm’s products from the threat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a firm can only avoid the threat of cannabilization by increasing capacity and/or revising the pricing strategy of both the green and brown products.
cannibalization is an unavoidable phenomenon when a firm introduces a new product to the market, but a two-level pricing scheme can help a firm to avoid cannibalizing its existing product line.
cannibalization is not a foregone conclusion when a company launches a green product.
